Q: Spring Security JWT user becoming null A:

I solved the issue by debugging the application. While debugging, I inspected the token being received in the SecurityFilter and analyzed its contents. I noticed that the token being sent during login was not the expected one generated by the application, but a different token. This caused the validation to fail and the user to be null. After discovering this, I searched where the incorrect token was being set in the system and removed it from the request. Once I removed the wrong token, the problem was resolved.

Q: How can I make a custom programming language run closer to C-level performance? A:

What makes a language slower is memory management. Python is garbage-collected, this is why it can never match C-level performance. Rust has manual memory management and can sometimes beat C performance.

Q: Make this code shorter and more optimized? DL 3155E24 || I/0 03 A:

8086 and 8088 are identical except for their memory interface (data bus being 16 and 8-bit wide respectively) and code-prefetch buffer size (6 and 4 bytes respectively: https://www.righto.com/2024/03/8088-prefetch-circuitry.html - Ken Shirriff has pretty much fully reverse-engineered 8086 by now.)

One memory access takes 4 cycles on either, but on 8086 it can access a whole aligned word, instead of just a single byte.

This makes code-fetch a huge bottleneck on 8088 since many instructions are at least 2 bytes, and simple operations that just work in registers often have cycle cost less than 4 cycles. Still somewhat of a bottleneck on 8086.

But 8088 was cheaper and didn't need as many pins for a memory bus, so IBM used it for the PC-XT, so that's what most people had back in the day, apparently.

I learned assembly on an Atari Mega 4 STe, Motorala 68000 CPU. (Actually 68020.) My dad had some m68k assembly books. I was messing around with a Mandelbrot fractal generator, with source code I typed in from another book, and obviously that has one small loop which is very hot. GCC runs pretty slowly on an Atari, even with a hard drive, so I started editing the compiler-generated asm instead of the C source, to see how fast I could make it run. You can still do the equivalent these days on a modern PC (preferably running Linux), although it's a lot harder to beat compilers and modern CPUs are a lot more complex. Still, seeing what compilers do is a great way to learn. See Matt Godbolt's CPPCon 2017 talk: “What Has My Compiler Done for Me Lately? Unbolting the Compiler's Lid”. See also How to remove "noise" from GCC/clang assembly output? re: writing functions that have interesting asm to look at.

I knew some electronics and digital logic from hobby stuff before I started programming, so I could see how simple I/O interfaces like a parallel port or joystick port could work.

And I found it pretty easy to see how lowish-level procedural imperative languages like C could directly map to assembly operations. Especially for C which was designed to make that possible. (Especially if you ignore the complexity of x86-16 real-mode segmentation. I luckily never had a 16-bit x86 as my home computer: I went straight from m68k Atari to Linux on a Pentium-MMX. No MS-DOS / BIOS brain-rot.)

I also took a course on assembly in undergrad, which focused on RISC architectures like MIPS. So I learned about pipelining, and read lots of stuff online about how CPUs work internally before I ever did much looking at x86 asm, like articles on https://www.realworldtech.com . Understanding a 5-stage classic RISC pipeline is interesting. See Modern Microprocessors A 90-Minute Guide! (which is excellent in general, not just about classic in-order RISC) and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic_RISC_pipeline

For more x86 asm guides, see https://stackoverflow.com/tags/x86/info
For performance stuff (for CPUs that aren't ancient), see https://agner.org/optimize/ and other CPU-architecture links from the tag wiki. For ancient stuff like 8086, see retrocomputing Q&As like https://retrocomputing.stackexchange.com/questions/17038/8086-duration-of-program/17048#17048
